solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: & 4, 21 Alarming Epstein files involved arrangements of adults with children (6)

indicators.note: people who are involved are tangled up with one another, and tangled letters keep none of the order they came in

blocks.note: twenty letters, the whole phrase redealt across three entries

explanation.surface: Released Epstein files turn out to describe, alarmingly, how adults were paired up with children.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole tail of the clue and does the misdirection by itself: a phrase that sounds like the scandal and means the ordinary household. The answer runs 1, 4, then 21.
explanation.definitionFit: Single-parent families are homes where one adult is raising the children, which is one very common arrangement of adults with children.

clue.text: Resilience shown by American going after male in disgrace (7)

indicators.note: a letter put in a word sits inside it, the word splitting to take it
what goes after the rest is written behind it, so this letter takes the last square

blocks.note: a stain on someone's name is a disgrace
m = male, the letter on any official form
a = American

explanation.surface: An American keeps on the heels of a man who is in disgrace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going after' poses as pursuit and is an instruction about position. Two of the three pieces are single letters, so the only whole word to find is the one behind 'disgrace'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stamina is the staying power that keeps you going long after it stops being comfortable, which is resilience of the physical kind.

clue.text: Fingers celebs (5)

blocks.note: to finger someone is to point them out, the informer's job
the big ones are the famous people themselves

explanation.surface: An informer points out which celebrities were in on it.
explanation.walkthrough: A two-word clue is nearly always two definitions, because there is no room for anything else. One half wants a verb and the other a plural noun, and the same five letters serve both.
explanation.definitionFit: To name someone is to finger them to the authorities, and a big name is a celebrity, so both halves are everyday uses of the one word.

clue.text: Dog with lead on biting children, right? (7)

indicators.note: to bite into something is to close your teeth round it, so the biting word shuts on both sides of what it takes

blocks.note: to lead someone on is to lure them
ch = children, as on a price list
r = right

explanation.surface: A dog held on its lead is snapping at passing children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' is the leash in the surface and the verb to entice in the wordplay, which is where the whole four-letter chunk comes from. A lurcher is a greyhound crossed with a working dog, long the poacher's dog in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A lurcher is a crossbred sighthound kept for hunting rabbits and hares, so 'dog' names it by kind.

clue.text: see 1ac.
Topless bar with US-style jugs for strong drink (6)

indicators.note: in a down entry the top is the first letter, and a topless word has lost it

blocks.note: BAR without the B it stands on
rack is American slang for a woman's breasts, the jugs of the surface

explanation.surface: A topless bar serving American-sized jugs of something fierce.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the wordplay are seedy on purpose, and the only instruction is the one hiding in 'topless'. Arrack is the fiery spirit distilled from palm sap or sugarcane across South and South-East Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrack is a spirit of forty per cent and upwards drunk from India to Indonesia, so 'strong drink' covers it plainly.

clue.text: Sexy rogue one's screwing (9)

indicators.note: a screw turns as it goes in, and letters given a turn come out in a different order

blocks.note: nine letters, the apostrophe ignored as always

explanation.surface: The attractive scoundrel somebody is currently sleeping with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' looks like idle grammar and hands over four of the nine letters. 'Sexy' stands alone at the front, which leaves every other word in the clue doing wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An erogenous zone is one that responds to sexual touch, so the adjective means sexually charged rather than good-looking.

clue.text: Sink party after misguided trope (7)

indicators.note: the party comes after the rest, so its two letters take the closing squares
something misguided has been pointed the wrong way, and letters pointed the wrong way land out of order

blocks.note: the five letters of TROPE reset
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A party goes under after somebody reaches for the wrong worn-out phrase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sink' works in both readings at once, the ship that goes down and the plan that is wrecked. 'Do' for a party is everyday British and the commonest two-letter charade piece there is.
explanation.definitionFit: To torpedo a scheme is to sink it, and the word keeps its naval sense too, so the verb fits either way.

clue.text: Prince in group with sex instigated by bloke with boat – fair play (13)

indicators.note: a prince put in a word is surrounded by it, that word opening to take him
to instigate something is to start it off, so what is wanted is the letter the word starts on

blocks.note: a sort is a kind or group of things
p = prince
the first letter of Sex, the one instigating it asks for
a bloke is a man
a ship is a boat to everyone except a sailor

explanation.surface: A prince joins a group for sex, egged on by a bloke who has a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points straight at the Epstein story, which is what makes the definition land where it does. 'Instigated' looks like a whole man's doing and asks only for one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Sportsmanship is playing by the rules and taking the result without complaint, which is fair play under another name.

clue.text: Royal home – ousted royal, abject, low, starts missing comfort (4)

indicators.note: the start of a word is the letter it opens on, one from each word listed
what is missing has gone from the word it sat in, and the rest closes up

blocks.note: Balmoral, the monarch's castle in Aberdeenshire and the family's summer house
the letters Ousted, Royal, Abject and Low start on, which the castle then loses from its end

explanation.surface: A royal turned out of the family home, brought low and badly in need of consolation.
explanation.walkthrough: Four words in a row give up their first letters, and the string they spell is the part to throw away rather than keep. 'Royal' earns its keep twice, once in each half of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A balm soothes a wound or a mood, so the noun stands for comfort itself rather than for anything that provides it.

clue.text: Range of skills of i.e. reporter rubbished (10)

indicators.note: to rubbish something is to tear it apart, and torn-up letters go back together any way at all

blocks.note: ten letters, the full stops dropped

explanation.surface: A reporter's abilities are being publicly rubbished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I.e.' earns nothing in the sentence, and a word that contributes nothing to the surface is usually contributing letters. Here it lends the first two of the ten.
explanation.definitionFit: A repertoire is the stock of pieces or tricks a performer can call on at will, which is a range of skills.

clue.text: Keir's heading off shit going round college – "Trash!" (6)

indicators.note: the heading of a word is the letter at its front
food gone off has turned, and letters that have turned no longer sit in the order they were given
one lot of letters going round another wraps it, splitting apart to take it in

blocks.note: the first letter of Keir, as in the Labour prime minister Keir Starmer
the four letters reset, ready to close round the next one
c = college

explanation.surface: Keir is walking out as filth circulates round a college, and someone calls it all trash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keir's heading off' reads as one man leaving and is two separate jobs, the heading wanted and the order of what follows destroyed. Only the K survives of his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Kitsch is showy, sentimental, tasteless stuff, the cheap ornament somebody dismisses as trash.

clue.text: Took off dress and celebrated pulling females (8)

indicators.note: to pull something is to draw it out, and once a letter is drawn out the rest closes up

blocks.note: a frock is a dress
someone celebrated has been feted
f = female, and one is pulled from each of the two words, leaving ROCK and ETED

explanation.surface: Somebody whips off a dress and celebrates having pulled a few women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulling females' is the chat-up sense in the surface and a removal in the parse, the same letter walking out of two different words. 'Took off' is the flight sense, not the undressing one.
explanation.definitionFit: A rocket takes off by leaving the ground fast, and prices or careers that rocketed took off the same way.

clue.text: Bum spots first signs of panicky president blocking vote – over-hasty (5,4)

indicators.note: the first sign of a word is the letter it opens with, one taken from each
something blocking a word is stuck in the middle of it, the word parting to make room

blocks.note: a nay is a vote against, the one recorded opposite aye
the first letters of Panicky and President
a rash decision is an over-hasty one

explanation.surface: A panicking president is blocking the vote and being reckless about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum spots' sits at the front doing the defining while everything after it paints a political scene. A nay is the vote recorded against, which is the only sense that gives up letters here.
explanation.definitionFit: Nappy rash is the red soreness a baby gets under its nappy, and under the nappy is exactly where the bum is.

clue.text: Leader there around island with duke (9)

indicators.note: what goes around a thing closes on both sides of it

blocks.note: someone there is present
i = island, as marked on charts
d = duke

explanation.surface: A leader tours an island in the company of a duke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'There' looks like the least useful word in the sentence and is the seven-letter chunk everything else fits into. The island and the duke are one letter each, dropped in side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A president heads a republic, a company or a club, so 'leader' is the bare job description.

clue.text: Start to crap in toilet (potty) (4)

indicators.note: the start of a word is the letter it opens on
a letter put in a word goes inside it, the word splitting round it

blocks.note: the loo is the British toilet
the first letter of Crap

explanation.surface: Somebody settling down to a crap in the toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: The brackets make 'potty' look like an aside about the lavatory when it is the definition, meaning mad. Loco came into English from Spanish, where it means exactly that.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone loco is out of their mind, which is what potty means in British English.

clue.text: Police coming back to arrest husband and other people (4)

indicators.note: something coming back arrives the other way round, last letter first
to arrest a thing is to stop it and hold it, so the holder closes round what it takes

blocks.note: the Met is London's police force, here set down from its last letter back
h = husband, the genealogist's shorthand

explanation.surface: Police on their way back pick up a husband and a few others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming back' does duty as the officers returning and as the instruction to read the force backwards. The Met is the Metropolitan Police, the crossword's standard force.
explanation.definitionFit: Them is the pronoun for everyone outside your own group, so 'other people' is what it means whenever it is set against us.

clue.text: One you can’t trust with property and gold (7)

blocks.note: a property in the sense of a characteristic is a trait
or = gold in heraldry, the tincture named on a shield

explanation.surface: A man who can be left alone with neither your possessions nor your gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Property' is possessions in the surface and a quality in the wordplay, the sense in 'the properties of a metal'. Heraldry's or for gold is worth learning early, because setters never signal it.
explanation.definitionFit: A traitor betrays the side that trusted them, so 'one you can't trust' is the warning given about them.

clue.text: Send email that's rehashed euphemism for predatory males? (6,3)

definitions.note: The definition does not give a synonym but names what the answer is: the polite phrase such men get described by.

indicators.note: a rehash serves the same material up in a new form, and letters served up again need not keep their places

blocks.note: nine letters, the message and the instruction to send it

explanation.surface: An old email is reworded and sent out again.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the definition as a euphemism, a phrase that sounds courtly and is used to cover for men who are nothing of the kind. Everything before 'that's' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A ladies' man is flattered as charming with women, which is the soft label the clue says is covering for something worse.

clue.text: Frantically question having ball amputated for examination (7)

indicators.note: a frantic person cannot keep still, and letters that will not keep still can land anywhere
an amputated part has been cut off, and it is gone from whatever is left

blocks.note: the eight letters as they stand, before the cut
o = ball, the round shape the letter draws, and it is the letter amputated here

explanation.surface: Frantic questioning of a patient who has had a ball cut off, all for examination.
explanation.walkthrough: The crude reading of 'ball amputated' is the surface's business; the instruction underneath is to drop one round letter before the shuffle. An inquest is the coroner's hearing, held in Britain whenever a death needs explaining.
explanation.definitionFit: An inquest is the formal inquiry into how someone died, and a formal inquiry is an examination of the facts.

clue.text: Predator primarily involved with teen is a predator no more (7)

definitions.note: The definition points at a particular person rather than giving a synonym, and 'no more' is the part that says which one: the dead one.

indicators.note: what comes primarily is the letter a word leads with
things involved with one another are tangled together, and tangled letters lose the order they came in

blocks.note: the leading letter of Predator
six letters, the little verb counted in

explanation.surface: A predator got tangled up with a teenager and is no longer any danger to anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'predator' does a job at each end of the clue, handing over its first letter at the front and defining at the back. 'No more' carries the plain sense: he is dead.
explanation.definitionFit: Jeffrey Epstein was the American financier convicted as a sex offender who died in his New York cell in 2019, so a predator no more.

clue.text: Order cocaine from idiot – twat dismissive of women (6)

indicators.note: taking one thing from another leaves the other short by exactly that much
to dismiss something is to send it away, so that letter leaves the word it was in

blocks.note: a dick is an idiot
c = cocaine, the letter taken out of the idiot
the four letters as they stand, before the cut
w = women, the letter dismissed from the word before it

explanation.surface: Scoring cocaine off an idiot, a twat with no time for women.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are built the same way, a crude word for a person minus the letter another word names. 'Order' at the front is the noun, the decree, not the verb the surface wants.
explanation.definitionFit: A diktat is an order handed down and not up for discussion, the sort nobody is invited to vote on.

clue.text: see 1 ac (8)
Sick question you texted: "Sexually available?" (6)

indicators.note: a word texted is spelt the short way, by the single letter that sounds like it

blocks.note: q = question
u = you, the way a phone spells it
someone called easy is being described as sexually available

explanation.surface: A text message puts a blunt question about how available somebody is.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon and the quotation marks dress the last two words up as the message being sent, when they are the last four letters. 'Sick' is the nauseous sense, not the slang one.
explanation.definitionFit: To feel queasy is to feel sick in the stomach, the turning feeling rather than any actual illness.

clue.text: Contact 19's top guy on the phone (5)

indicators.note: in a down entry the top of a word is the letter it starts on
a word said down a phone reaches the ear as sound alone, with no spelling attached to it

blocks.note: the letter the answer to 19 down begins with
a guy is a male, and said aloud that is the postal word instead

explanation.surface: Getting hold of the man at the top of 19 by telephone.
explanation.walkthrough: A cross-reference gives letters like any other word, and this one gives just the letter its answer starts on. 'On the phone' is the sound instruction and 'Contact' the verb being defined.
explanation.definitionFit: To email someone is to contact them, a verb the word now does as readily as it does duty as a noun.

clue.text: Experienced "bastard" setter is in Private Eye (10)

indicators.note: a bastard thing is of mixed and irregular parentage, and letters of mixed parentage turn up in any order
a word put in another sits inside it, that word opening to take it

blocks.note: the six letters of SETTER reset
the magazine this crossword appears in, speaking of itself the way every paper does
lifted off the page as it stands and dropped inside

explanation.surface: A setter with a reputation as a bastard writes for Private Eye.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a true statement about itself, which is how the magazine comes to supply its own 'we'. The quotation marks round 'bastard' hint that the word is not doing the job it appears to.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone streetwise has picked up how things really work by living among them, which is experience of the hard-won kind.

clue.text: Means to pay a married old lover (4)

blocks.note: the article taken off the page as the letter it is
m = married, as on a form
an ex is an old flame

explanation.surface: Finding a way to pay off a married former lover.
explanation.walkthrough: Amex is the everyday short form of American Express, the charge card. The 'a' earns a letter of its own, which is easy to miss while it is posing as plain grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: An Amex is an American Express card, so producing one at the till is a means to pay.

clue.text: Spin (or backtracking?) by misogynist (6)

indicators.note: to backtrack is to go back the way you came, so those letters are read in reverse

blocks.note: the word OR taken off the page and turned round
Andrew Tate, the influencer whose online following was built on contempt for women

explanation.surface: A misogynist puts his own spin on things, or else quietly goes back on them.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed aside looks like the setter offering a second thought and is the instruction: the little word in front of the question mark goes back the way it came.
explanation.definitionFit: To rotate is to turn on an axis, which is what anything spinning is doing.

clue.text: "Lost out!" – Ghislaine, when finally nicked (6)

indicators.note: what is out is out of true, and letters knocked out of true can be set down in any order
the final letter of a word is the one it ends on

blocks.note: the four letters of LOST reset
the letters GhislainE and wheN finish on

explanation.surface: Ghislaine complains that she has lost out, now that she has finally been arrested.
explanation.walkthrough: Ghislaine Maxwell, jailed in 2021 for supplying girls to Epstein, is the Ghislaine meant. 'Nicked' is British for arrested, which is the surface, and for taken without asking, which is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicked is British slang for taken without permission, which is exactly what has happened to anything stolen.
